01.note: Rav Huna kept rams that needed shade during the day and fresh air at night, so their pen had to be covered by day and open by night, Shabbat included. He came to Rav for advice. Rav told him to roll up the mats that shaded the pen but leave one handbreadth still spread; the next day he could unroll the whole mat, since that only adds to a temporary tent that already exists, which is permitted.
01.why: The Gemara has just quoted Rav Asi: over boat arches a handbreadth wide, a mat may be spread on Shabbat because it only adds to a temporary tent. Rav's advice applies the same principle to an animal pen.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Owner of the rams, who asks Rav how to shade them by day and air them by night.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage Rav Huna consults; he tells him to leave a handbreadth of the mat spread.

terms.meaning: A roof put up for a short time. Building a new one on Shabbat is forbidden, but adding to one that already stands is allowed, which is why leaving a handbreadth in place before Shabbat matters.
A unit of measure, roughly the width of a palm (about 8 to 10 cm). A covering of at least this width counts as a roof in Jewish law.

02.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi recalls standing before his father, Rav Ashi, when his father's bandage fell onto a pillow and he put it back on. The son asked whether he did not hold by Rav Hisda's teaching that the dispute concerns only a bandage that fell onto a utensil, together with Shmuel's ruling that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda. His father answered, "I did not hear this," which the Gemara explains as meaning "I do not agree."
02.why: A baraita disputes whether a bandage that came off may be replaced on Shabbat; Rav Hisda limited the dispute to one that fell onto a utensil, and Shmuel ruled with Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Ashi's conduct shows he rejected Rav Hisda's limit and allowed putting the bandage back.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Son of Rav Ashi, who tells the story and questions his father.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: The father, called simply Father here, who replaces his fallen bandage on Shabbat.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Sage whose teaching limits the dispute to a bandage that fell onto a utensil.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Sage who ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Sage of the earlier baraita whose opinion Shmuel says is the law.

terms.meaning: The binding Jewish law on a question, as opposed to an opinion that was argued but not adopted.

03.note: Ulla was visiting the house of Rav Menashe when a man came and knocked at the door. Ulla said: "Who is that? May his body be desecrated, as he desecrates Shabbat," because knocking makes a sound. The story ends with Ulla's curse; the reply comes in the discussion that follows.
03.why: The mishna allows drawing water with a noisy wheel only in the Temple, and the Gemara is asking whether making any sound is forbidden on Shabbat. Rabba answers Ulla that only a pleasant musical sound was forbidden, and Abaye then challenges him.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: A Sage visiting Rav Menashe's house, who curses the man knocking on the door.

people.name: Rav Menashe
people.about: The host whose house Ulla is visiting.

terms.meaning: Breaks one of the rules of the Sabbath rest. Here Ulla holds that even producing a sound by knocking counts.

03.flag: The story stops at Ulla's curse; Rabba's reply to him, which completes the exchange, falls outside the story.

04.note: Ameimar allowed the people of Mehoza to draw water on Shabbat with a wheel. He reasoned that the Sages forbade it only in case someone drew water for his garden or his ruin, and Mehoza had neither gardens nor ruins. But once he saw that they were soaking flax in the water, he forbade them to use the wheel.
04.why: The Gemara has just explained that the mishna limits wheel-drawing to the Temple because of a decree: a person might go on to water his garden. Ameimar's ruling tests that reason in a town where it seemed not to apply.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: A Sage who first permits and then forbids drawing water by wheel in Mehoza.

terms.meaning: A rule the Sages added to protect people from breaking a Torah law by accident. Here the worry is that someone using the wheel would also water his garden, which is forbidden work on Shabbat.
Steeping flax plants in water to loosen the fibers for linen. Doing it on Shabbat is forbidden work, so drawing water for it was a real risk.

05.note: Three priests in the Temple each received a small share of the showbread divided among the priests. One said he got a portion the size of a bean, one said the size of an olive, and the third said the size of a lizard's tail. They investigated the third priest's background and found a trace of disqualification in him.
05.why: This is one of a run of stories about the importance of clean, fitting speech. The Gemara then asks how his lineage could be investigated beyond the altar, and reads the finding as arrogance, or as his casting suspicion on himself.

terms.meaning: Twelve loaves set out each week on a table in the Temple and then divided among the priests to eat.
A lizard is one of the creeping creatures the Torah calls ritually impure, so comparing holy bread to one was an unfitting image for a priest.
A defect, usually in family lineage, that makes a man unfit to serve as a priest.

06.note: A gentile kept going up to Jerusalem and eating the Paschal lamb, boasting that despite the verses barring foreigners he ate the finest portions. Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira asked whether they had fed him the fat tail; he said no, and the Sage told him to ask for it next time. When he did, the others told him the fat tail goes up to God on the altar. They asked who told him to ask; he said Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira. They investigated, found he was a gentile, and killed him. Then they sent word: "Peace unto you, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, as you are in Netzivin and your net is spread in Jerusalem."
06.why: The Gemara has just discussed investigating a priest's lineage and how far such checks go; this story shows an investigation of someone's origins that the Sage set in motion from afar.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
people.about: A Sage living in Netzivin who tricks the gentile into asking for the fat tail.

terms.meaning: The lamb sacrificed in the Temple on the eve of Passover and eaten that night. The Torah forbids it to foreigners and to uncircumcised men.
The fatty tail of the sheep. It is burned on the altar, never eaten, so anyone asking for it showed he did not know the rules.

07.note: Rav Kahana fell ill, and the Sages sent Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi, to see how he was. He found that Rav Kahana had died. He tore his garment, turned it so the tear was behind him, and came back crying. They asked him, "Did he die?" He answered, "I did not say that," quoting the verse "And he who utters slander is a fool."
07.why: This is one of a run of stories praising careful speech. The Gemara presents it as an example of avoiding being the one who announces bad news outright.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who falls ill and dies.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: Sent by the Sages to check on Rav Kahana; he lets them understand the death without saying it.

terms.meaning: Tearing one's clothing is the traditional Jewish sign of mourning on hearing of a death.

08.note: Yohanan from Hakuk went out to the villages. When he came back, people asked him whether the wheat had grown well. Not wanting to say no, he answered that the barley had grown well. They mocked him: "Go out and tell the horses and donkeys," since Scripture calls barley food for horses. The Gemara asks what he should have said, and answers: that last year's wheat grew well, or that the lentils grew well.
08.why: This is another in a run of stories about clean speech and avoiding bad news; here the attempt fails because the hint is unflattering.

people.name: Yohanan from Hakuk
people.about: A man asked about the wheat harvest who answers indirectly about the barley.

09.note: Rabbi Yehuda reports that the maidservant of a violent man in the city of Rimon threw a stillborn baby into a pit. A priest came and looked into the pit to see whether it was male or female. The case came before the Sages, and they ruled the priest ritually pure, because martens and polecats are common there and had likely dragged the body away.
09.why: Rava had held that an uncertainty cannot override a certainty. The Gemara cites this case against him, since a certain corpse seems overridden by an uncertain animal, and then offers readings that save his rule.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage in the baraita who reports the incident.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.
Free of the impurity that, for example, contact with or standing over a corpse brings. A priest must avoid such impurity.
The mother's period of impurity after a birth, even a stillbirth, differs for a boy and a girl, which is why the priest wanted to know.

10.note: Someone left a saddlebag full of leavened bread with Yohanan Hakuka'a. Mice bored a hole in it and the bread was spilling out. On the eve of Passover he came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who told him at the first hour to wait, and again at the second, third and fourth. At the fifth hour he told him to go and sell it in the market. Rav Yosef and Abaye then argue whether the sale was meant for gentiles or for Jews, and Rav Adda bar Mattana reminds Rav Yosef that he had once said explicitly: sell it to gentiles.
10.why: The Gemara is asking until what hour leaven may be eaten on Passover eve. The story is brought to show that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi also held, like Rabbi Yehuda, that Jews may no longer eat it in the fifth hour.

people.name: Yohanan Hakuka'a
people.about: The man holding the deposited saddlebag of leaven who asks what to do.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who tells him to wait hour by hour, then to sell it.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Sage who first suggests the sale was to Jews.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Sage who asks why, if so, the man did not keep the leaven himself.

people.name: Rav Adda bar Mattana
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who reminds him he once said it was to be sold to gentiles.

terms.meaning: Bread or dough that has risen. Jews may not eat or own it on Passover, and from a set hour on the day before, it must be gone.
The daylight hours counted from morning. The Sages disagree whether leaven may still be eaten in the fifth hour before it becomes forbidden in the sixth.
Officials who gather money or food for the poor. The baraita says they sell to others, not to themselves, so no one suspects them.

11.note: Shimon HaAmmassoni, or by another account Nehemya HaAmmassoni, used to draw a new teaching from every occurrence of the little word "et" in the Torah. When he reached "You shall be in awe of the Lord your God," he stopped. His students asked what would become of all the ones he had already explained. He said: just as I received reward for the interpretation, I shall receive reward for withdrawing. The verse stayed unexplained until Rabbi Akiva taught that its "et" includes Torah scholars.
11.why: The Gemara has just said that one Sage does not interpret the word "et" at all. This baraita shows where that view comes from: the Sage who once expounded every "et" gave the method up.

people.name: Shimon HaAmmassoni
people.about: A Sage who expounded every "et" in the Torah until he reached the verse about fearing God; some say his name was Nehemya HaAmmassoni.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Sage who later explained that verse's "et" as including Torah scholars.

terms.meaning: A short Hebrew word that marks the object of a verb and has no meaning of its own in translation. Some Sages read it as a hint to include something more.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

12.note: Mar bar Rav Ashi found Ravina rubbing his daughter with unripe olives of orla to treat her. He asked him: the Sages allowed benefit from such forbidden things at a time of danger, but who said so when there is no danger? Ravina answered that a high fever also counts as a time of danger. Some say he answered instead that he was not using the olives in the usual way of benefit.
12.why: The Gemara is discussing which prohibitions may be set aside to heal a person, ruling that only idolatry, forbidden relations and murder may not be. This case asks how far a lesser prohibition yields when life is not clearly at risk.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Sage who questions Ravina's use of forbidden olives.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage who treats his daughter with olives of orla and defends doing so.

terms.meaning: Fruit from a tree in its first three years after planting. The Torah forbids not only eating it but any benefit from it.
A situation where life may be at risk. Most Torah prohibitions are set aside to save a life.

13.note: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok tells how he once followed his father, Rabbi Tzadok, into Rabban Gamliel's home on Passover, and they were served matza shaped in figures. He asked: "Father, didn't the Sages say one may not make shaped matza on Passover?" His father answered: "My son, they did not say this for everyone's matza, only for bakers' matza."
13.why: A baraita says shaped matza should not be baked on Passover because the delay may let the dough rise. The story narrows that rule; the Gemara then gives a second version in which it applies to ordinary people and not to bakers.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok
people.about: Tells the story; he asks his father about the shaped matza.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: His father, who explains whose shaped matza the Sages forbade.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The host in whose home the shaped matza was served.

terms.meaning: Flat unleavened bread eaten on Passover. The dough must be baked before it begins to rise.
Matza decorated with shapes or designs. Making the figures takes time, during which the dough might rise.

14.note: Rabbi Ilai asked Rabbi Eliezer whether a person can fulfill the duty of eating matza with the loaves of a thanks-offering or a nazirite's wafers. Rabbi Eliezer said he had not heard. Rabbi Ilai went to Rabbi Yehoshua, who said: loaves a man made for his own offering do not count, but ones baked to sell in the market do. When Rabbi Ilai reported this back, Rabbi Eliezer exclaimed, "By the covenant, these are the very matters stated to Moses at Sinai." Some say he said it in astonishment, asking whether a rule like that does not need a reason.
14.why: The Gemara is discussing why these offering loaves cannot be used as Passover matza. This baraita gives the distinction between loaves for oneself and loaves for sale, and the Gemara then asks for its reason.

people.name: Rabbi Ilai
people.about: The Sage who asks the question and carries the answer back.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Sage who first says he has not heard, then reacts to Rabbi Yehoshua's answer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Sage who answers, distinguishing loaves made for oneself from loaves for sale.

terms.meaning: A sacrifice brought to thank God, accompanied by several kinds of loaves, some of them unleavened.
Unleavened wafers brought with the offerings of a nazirite, a person who took a vow to abstain from wine and haircuts for a period.

terms.term: matters stated to Moses at Sinai
terms.meaning: A phrase for a law handed down by tradition from Moses rather than derived from a verse.

15.note: Rav Mattana taught in the town of Paphunya that a woman should knead matza only with water that rested. The next day everyone came to him with their jugs and said, "Give us water," taking his words to mean his own water. He told them he meant water that had rested in the house overnight.
15.why: Rav Yehuda has just ruled that matza dough may be kneaded only with water left overnight to cool. The story shows how the wording of that ruling was misheard.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: Sage who taught the ruling in Paphunya and was misunderstood.

terms.meaning: Water left indoors overnight to cool, so warm water does not make the matza dough rise. In Hebrew the phrase sounds almost like "our water", which caused the mix-up.
Flat unleavened bread eaten on Passover. The dough must be baked before it begins to rise.

16.note: A man from the Land of Israel visited Babylonia carrying meat, and asked his hosts to bring him a dip for his bread. He heard them say, "Bring him kutah." As soon as he heard the word kutah, he stopped eating.
16.why: A baraita explains that the Sages listed foods containing grain by name so people would learn their names. This incident shows why knowing what a food is called matters.

terms.meaning: A Babylonian dip or relish that contains milk, so it may not be eaten with meat under Jewish dietary law.
Babylonian Sages called the Land of Israel the West, since it lay west of Babylonia.

17.note: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok recalls that his father, Rabbi Tzadok, spent Shabbat in Yavne one year when the fourteenth of Nisan fell on Shabbat. Zonin, Rabban Gamliel's appointee, came and announced that the time had come to remove leavened bread, and father and son went and removed it.
17.why: The mishna records a dispute over when to remove leaven when the day before Passover is Shabbat: before Shabbat, at the usual time, or split. The story supports removing it at the usual time even on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok
people.about: Tells the story; he went with his father to remove the leaven.

people.name: Zonin
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's appointee, who announces the time for removing leaven.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The leader whose appointee makes the announcement in Yavne.

terms.meaning: The day before Passover, when all leaven must be gone from one's home by a set hour.
A collection of early teachings from the time of the Mishna, often quoted in the Gemara.

18.note: Rav Idi bar Avin married the daughter of a priest, and two sons ordained as Sages came from him: Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi, and Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi. Likewise Rav Pappa said: had I not married a daughter of a priest, I would not have become wealthy.
18.why: Rabbi Yohanan had said marrying a priest's daughter can be inauspicious, and the Gemara explained that it is so for an ignoramus but brings blessing to a Torah scholar. These cases show the blessing; Rav Kahana then reports a bad outcome.

people.name: Rav Idi bar Avin
people.about: Married a priest's daughter and had two sons who became ordained Sages.

people.name: Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi
people.about: One of the two ordained sons.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua, son of Rav Idi
people.about: The other ordained son.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who credits his wealth to marrying a priest's daughter.

terms.meaning: Formally authorized to decide questions of Jewish law.

18.flag: Not much of a story: two brief reports of marriages and their results, with no events beyond that.

19.note: Rabbi Akiva said that when he was an ignoramus he used to say: "Who will give me a Torah scholar, so that I will bite him like a donkey?" His students said, "Master, say like a dog!" He answered that a donkey bites and breaks bones, while a dog bites but does not break bones.
19.why: The Gemara is gathering harsh sayings of the Sages about ignoramuses and their hostility; Rabbi Akiva gives the view from the other side, recalling his own hatred of scholars before he learned.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Recalls his hostility toward Torah scholars from the time he was an ignoramus.

terms.meaning: A person with no Torah learning. In this discussion the word describes people openly hostile to scholars.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.

20.note: Rav Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, fell ill and came close to death. When he recovered, his father asked what he had seen. He said he saw an inverted world: those above were below, and those below above. His father said, "My son, you have seen a clear world," and asked where scholars like themselves stood there. Rav Yosef answered that they are regarded there just as here. He added that he heard them say: praiseworthy is one who arrives with his learning in hand, and no one can stand in the enclosure of those executed by the government.
20.why: The Gemara is expounding Zechariah's words about light that is precious and dim. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads them as people important in this world who are lowly in the next, and his son's vision illustrates that reading.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: Comes close to death and reports what he saw of the next world.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
people.about: His father, who asks him what he saw.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, where, in the Sages' view, people receive their true reward.
Martyrs put to death by the ruling power. The Gemara goes on to ask who exactly is meant.
